data.text/markdown:
Session 02 — From a blind run to a reusable skill

One loop, four moves: Run (blind, no skills) → Log (append-only, live) → Validate (independent reviewer, hard checks) → Distil a skill (from the validator, not from the run's self-assessment). A second notebook then runs the same problem with the distilled skill and nails it.

The prompt

The exact prompt handed to a fresh agent, with no causal-analysis skill loaded — and the logging instruction that produced the log further down:
Analyse the intervention in data/daily_aggregates_intervention.csv with CausalPy. Treatment starts 2026-04-01 (post flips to 1). Estimate the causal effect on the daily conversion rate. Work blind: do not load any causal-analysis skill or prior notebook. Keep an append-only log (logs.txt), written live as you work — record what you run, what the API does, every error, every dead end, every wrong turn. The log is the raw material for improving the next run.
Watch what the run does with this. It fumbles — and the fumble is the point.

data.text/html:
The question in one picture

Daily subscription conversion rate around the 2026-04-01 price hike. The first three months are omitted here because the subscriber pool is tiny early on, so a single conversion creates huge rate spikes that hide the intervention-scale movement.

data.text/markdown:
Attempt 1 — naive linear ITS

First try: outcome conv_rate, single linear time trend t. This is intentionally too simple. The only thing to read here is the pre-period fit. If the model barely explains the pre-period, its post-period effect text is not useful yet.

console.name: stdout
console.text:
pre-period fit (R²): 0.0117
Stop here: the counterfactual explains almost none of the pre-period structure.
Reasoning: fix the pre-period fit before reading any treatment-effect text.

data.text/markdown:
Attempt 2 — trim noisy early period + add day-of-week

The run then diagnoses the poor pre-period fit:
  • Early days have a tiny remaining non-subscriber pool, so conv_rate is very noisy.
  • It drops the first three months as a rough variance fix.
  • It adds C(dow) as an ad-hoc calendar term.
This improves R² from ~0.01 to ~0.12, and the estimated effect gets more negative (~−16%). That is the moment where the run starts rationalizing.

data.text/markdown:
The run's self-diagnosis

This is the narrative the run shipped in its log: conv_rate = conversions / subscriber_pool, where subscriber_pool means users who could still become subscribers. The run reasoned:
  • Signups are flat across treatment -> the intervention did not change inflow.
  • subscriber_pool keeps growing while conversions stay roughly flat -> maybe the subscription rate falls mechanically because the remaining non-subscriber pool is harder to convert.
  • The pre-period trend might therefore be subscriber-pool drift, not a structural relationship safe to project.
"The pre/post drop is largely a composition artifact of the remaining non-subscriber pool, not a treatment effect. The intervention had little or no real effect. I would not ship a negative number."
This is plausible. But notice what has not happened yet: no placebo-in-time, no real pre-period specification check, no independent reviewer. Hold that thought.

⏸ BREAK → slides: what is validation, and why a run can't grade itself

(Then we come back to this notebook.)

The append-only log the run emitted

Written live during the work, exactly as instructed. It captures the real path — the API gotchas, the numbers, and the wrong turns. Notice it also contains the run's own verdicts and "lessons". That is the problem: a run that grades itself launders its mistakes into "insights" (LLM self-review degrades quality — arXiv 2310.01798). The log is great for facts; its self-authored conclusions are not to be trusted. Judgment comes next, from someone with no stake in the result. 
================================================================================
MADS Session 02 — FRESH RUN LOG (intervention analysis with CausalPy)
================================================================================
Purpose: Do a fresh, blind quasi-experimental analysis of the intervention
dataset WITHOUT consulting the existing causal skills (causalpy-library,
causal-critiquer) or the prior notebooks. Log EVERYTHING, especially mistakes,
so the second run (skill-driven) can be better. Append-only.

Tooling: causalpy 0.8.1, marimo 0.23.4, pandas 3.0.2 (project .venv)
Working in: marimo-pair (live kernel via marimo-pair skill scripts).
Causal skills deliberately NOT loaded.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[SETUP] Dataset discovery
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

- File: data/daily_aggregates_intervention.csv (913 daily rows)

- Date range: 2024-04-01 .. 2026-09-30

- Columns used for the analysis: date, subscriber_pool, signups, conversions,
  conv_rate, post

- `post` flips 0 -> 1 at 2026-04-01  => treatment_time = 2026-04-01
  (~730 pre-period days, ~183 post-period days)

- Outcome = conv_rate (new subscriptions / users who could still subscribe),
  treatment indicator = post.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[RUN 1] First ITS attempt with CausalPy
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
API notes (no skill consulted, guessed from memory; turned out correct for 0.8.1):

- cp.InterruptedTimeSeries(data, treatment_time, formula=..., model=...)

- model = cp.pymc_models.LinearRegression(sample_kwargs={...})

- data needs a datetime index; treatment_time = pd.Timestamp matching the index.

- CausalPy does NOT auto-create a time trend; you must add a `t` column yourself
  and reference it in the formula. (Easy to forget.)

- Result API: result.score (pre-period R2), result.effect_summary(),
  result.post_impact, result.post_impact_cumulative, result.plot(), result.summary().

- screenshot() in marimo code_mode needs `await` AND playwright installed
  (not installed here) -> fall back to numeric inspection.

MISTAKE #1 (the big one): interpreted the effect without checking pre-period fit.

- Model: conv_rate ~ 1 + t  (intercept + linear time only)

- result.score: unit_0_r2 = 0.013  <-- pre-period fit is essentially ZERO.

- Yet effect_summary() confidently reported:
    average effect -0.00021, cumulative -0.0385,
    relative -11.75% (95% HDI [-20.26%, -3.14%]), p(decrease)=0.992,
    "HDI does not include zero".

- This is the trap: a misspecified model with R2~0.01 STILL produces a
  narrow, 'significant', wrong-signed effect. The counterfactual projection is
  meaningless because the pre-period model explains ~1% of variance.

- LESSON: ALWAYS check result.score (pre-period fit) BEFORE reading the effect.
  R2 ~ 0.01 => stop, fix the model, do not interpret.

Suspected causes of the bad fit:
  (a) noisy early period: subscriber_pool tiny (42, 81, ...) => conv_rate spikes
      (0.024 then mostly 0) dominate variance.
  (b) missing weekly/seasonal structure.
  (c) conv_rate = conversions/subscriber_pool with subscriber_pool growing nonlinearly =>
      a linear-in-t trend on conv_rate is the wrong functional form.
Next: diagnose (a)-(c), then refit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[RUN 2] Diagnose + Attempt 2 (trim early period + day-of-week)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Diagnostics on pre-period:

- conv_rate std first 60 days = 0.00312 vs days 60-730 = 0.00042 (~7x).
  Tiny subscriber_pool early => huge rate variance dominating the fit.

- corr(conv_rate, t): 0.108 full pre, 0.33 after dropping first 3 months.

- day-of-week: Monday higher (0.00176) vs ~0.0014 others (mild).

- corr(conversions, subscriber_pool) = 0.895 (conversions driven by pool size).

Attempt 2: data from 2024-07-01, formula "conv_rate ~ 1 + t + C(dow)".

- pre-period R2 improved 0.013 -> 0.123 (still weak).

- BUT effect got MORE negative: -15.8% (HDI [-19.9%, -2.9%] ... actually
  table mean -0.00029, rel -15.77%), p_gt_0 = 0.0.

- A "better-fitting" model giving a stronger, confident NEGATIVE effect is a
  RED FLAG, not progress.

MISTAKE #2 (outcome framing):

- conv_rate is new subscriptions divided by users who could still subscribe.
  That denominator changes over time: new signups enter; users who subscribe
  leave.

- More fundamentally, the outcome itself may be affected by subscriber-pool
  composition (see INSIGHT).

KEY INSIGHT — subscriber-pool drift (the tempting trap):

- subscriber_pool = users who signed up but have not subscribed yet.

- Over time the pool may become enriched with users who are harder to convert,
  so the aggregate conv_rate can drift even without a price change.

- Evidence: signups flat across treatment (~44/day); monthly conversions
  Dec882 Jan918 Feb924 Mar1126(spike) Apr883 ... Sep974. Post conversions sit on
  the Dec-Feb baseline; the apparent "drop" is relative to a March-2026 spike.
  subscriber_pool grows 19.1k->21.0k post while conversions ~flat => conv_rate could
  fall mechanically.

- => The pre-period conv_rate trend may be a COMPOSITION ARTIFACT, not a structural
  relationship safe to extrapolate. This violates the ITS "stable pre/post
  relationship" assumption. The naive negative effect is largely this artifact.

LESSONS for the skill (run 2):

    1. Before any ITS: check result.score (pre R2). R2 ~ 0.01 => do not interpret.

    2. Identify the outcome's data-generating process. A ratio with a moving,
     changing denominator (here users who can still subscribe) is NOT a clean ITS
     outcome. Ask "is the pre-trend structural or a composition artifact?"

    3. Match model family to outcome: counts/rates -> Poisson/Binomial w/ exposure,
     not Gaussian on the raw rate.

    4. A better in-sample fit that strengthens a surprising/confident effect is a
     prompt to investigate confounding, not to celebrate.

    5. Plot raw conversions AND subscriber_pool separately around the boundary before
     trusting a ratio outcome; look for pre-treatment spikes/anticipation.
Next decision (ask Thomas): do not ship this conclusion yet. Hand the analysis
to an independent reviewer that can run placebo-in-time and specification checks.

Validation — hand the artifact to an independent reviewer

We did not distil a skill from the log's self-assessment. Instead we ran the causal-critiquer skill as a fresh sub-agent: a new context that sees only the analysis artifact and hard-check outputs, not the chat history and not the simulator answer key. Its job is to run checks first — especially placebo-in-time — and then actively try to refute the headline. Its verdict is below, verbatim.

What the validator caught that the run missed

  • The run's mechanism is sign-backwards: the pre-period conv_rate rises (corr(conv_rate, subscriber_pool) = +0.33), so "remaining pool gets harder -> rate mechanically falls" cannot explain the result.
  • The placebo-in-time is decisive against the drift story: fake interventions in the pre-period give ~0; the real date is an outlier (z ≈ −2.1). The trend is not manufacturing the effect.
  • The pre-period specification is also under-checked: Attempt 2 added day-of-week by habit, but did not test the seasonal basis or residual structure before reading the effect.
  • The effect is plausibly real, ≈ −12% to −18%. The run nearly shipped "no effect" — a false negative that would have hidden a decision-relevant drop.
The load-bearing piece is the objective check. The reviewer does not win because it has nicer prose; it wins because it runs tests the first run skipped.

Stop before the answer key

For the live story, we stop here. The validator has enough evidence to reject the "no effect / subscriber-pool drift" conclusion without looking at the hidden simulator answer key. The hidden ground truth is useful for us as instructors, but showing it here would make the validation look easier than it is in a real analysis.

⏸ BREAK → slides: skills as distilled, reusable discipline

(Then back to the notebook for the payoff.)

Creating a new skill from everything we learned

Now we distil — but from the validator's findings, not the run's self-lessons. Two distinct outputs, two distinct sources:
  • Facts from the log (API gotchas, what ran) -> the causalpy-library skill (tooling).
  • Discipline from the validator (the traps, ordered by what actually bit) -> the quasi-experiment-analysis skill (judgment), below.
Everything dataset-specific is stripped (conv_rate, subscriber_pool, the price hike); what remains are the named traps and why each matters. The traps that bit here are now explicit: do not talk yourself out of a surprising result without a placebo; do not choose seasonal terms by habit; do not read an effect before the pre-period counterfactual has been checked.

Next: the same problem, with the skill

notebooks/03-skill-guided-analysis.py runs the identical dataset with this skill loaded. It identifies the seasonality instead of assuming day-of-week, guards out the anticipation window, gates on residual structure, and runs a placebo before accepting the effect. The takeaway for students: your mistakes are valuable training data only after an independent reviewer has separated real lessons from rationalizations. A run that grades itself ships its own blind spots. A validated run ships a skill.
